opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's honestly one of the hardest parts of building in this space, and I think people underestimate how hard it is until they're in it.

The first layer is pretty conventional: we have internal task suites. These are sets of realistic things a person might actually want done on the web, like booking something, filling out a form, comparing products, tracking down a piece of information that's buried a few clicks deep. For each one we have some notion of what success looks like, and we track completion rates over time. Public benchmarks are useful as a sanity check too, but you have to be careful, because the web changes constantly. A site gets redesigned, a flow changes, and suddenly your number moves for reasons that have nothing to do with your agent. So we try to separate "the agent got worse" from "the world changed underneath us."

But end-to-end success alone is a pretty blunt instrument. If a task takes twenty steps and the agent fails, you want to know where and why. So we look at the trajectories themselves. Did it misread the page? Did it plan badly? Did it get stuck in a loop? Did it give up too early, or not ask the user for clarification when it really should have? Breaking failures down into categories like that tells you a lot more about what to work on next than a single success number does.

Then there's efficiency and reliability, which matter a lot for real users. An agent that eventually succeeds but takes ten minutes, or succeeds sometimes and not others on the same task, isn't one people will trust. So we look at the number of steps, time taken, and consistency across repeated runs.

And ultimately, the thing I care about most is whether it's actually useful to people. So we spend a lot of time just watching how people use it. What do they try to delegate? Where do they intervene? Do they come back? Those signals are messier, but they keep you honest. It's very easy to optimize a benchmark and not move the needle on whether someone's day actually got easier.

There's also a qualitative piece that I don't want to undersell: the team uses the agent themselves, a lot. You develop an intuition for whether it feels better or worse that sometimes runs ahead of what your metrics are capturing. When that intuition and the metrics disagree, that's usually a sign your evals are missing something, and that's a good prompt to go build a better eval.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's harder than it sounds, and I think that's one of the most underappreciated parts of building these systems. The temptation is to pick a benchmark, get a number, and watch it go up. But with web agents, the number can go up while the thing you actually care about isn't getting better at all.

So we try to look at it from a few angles. The first is task success on a held-out set of real tasks, things like "book this," "find that," "fill out this form," where the end state is actually checkable. Not "did the agent say it did it," but did the state of the world change the way it was supposed to. That distinction matters a lot, because these models are very good at narrating success.

The second is looking at how it fails, not just how often. If success goes from 60 to 65 percent but the new failures are things like taking an irreversible action it shouldn't have, or confidently doing the wrong thing on a page it misread, that's not an improvement in my book. So we bucket failures: couldn't find the element, misunderstood the task, got stuck in a loop, took an unsafe action. The shape of that distribution tells you more than the headline number.

Third, and this is where it gets uncomfortable, we spend a lot of time just watching trajectories. Sitting down and reading through what the agent did, step by step. It's slow and it doesn't scale, but every time we skip it we end up fooling ourselves. You see patterns that no metric captures, like the agent technically succeeding but taking thirty steps for something a person does in four.

And then the last piece is robustness. Does it still work when the site changes its layout a little, when there's a popup, when the network is slow? Because the real web is messy, and a system that only works on the static snapshot you evaluated on isn't really improving in any sense that matters to a user.

So if I had to summarize: a checkable outcome, a failure taxonomy, human eyes on trajectories, and some deliberate messiness in the evaluation. Any one of those alone will mislead you.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to evaluate it on the tasks you actually want it to accomplish. Can you give the agent a goal, have it interact with a website, and verify that it achieved that goal? Producing a plausible sequence of clicks isn’t enough; the resulting state has to be correct.

Then you want to understand how consistently it succeeds across different tasks and websites, how much human intervention it needs, and what it costs in time and computation. Looking at the failures is especially useful: did it misunderstand the instruction, miss something on the page, or struggle to recover after an action didn’t work? That helps distinguish an improvement on a benchmark from a system that’s becoming more useful and reliable.

r001.rationale: It contrasts a plausible sequence of clicks with verifying that the agent completed the goal and reached the correct state, distinguishing action behavior from task-level success.

r002.rationale: It discusses task success, consistency, intervention, cost, and failures, but does not identify the quality of the final user-facing report as a separate evaluation target.

sol-6.1.text: I think the key is to evaluate whether the agent actually accomplishes the user’s goal. Did it complete the task correctly, and how much human intervention did it need? You also want to look at efficiency—how many steps it took—and whether those improvements hold across a variety of tasks. A successful demonstration is useful, but what matters is whether the system becomes consistently more reliable.
